This review assesses how artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning (ML) and High-performance computing optimization, improves the efficiency of operational HPC systems. Approximately 1,800 publications from 2019 Software performance to 2025 were manually screened using predefined inclusion/exclusion criteria; 74 ‘‘AI for HPC’’ papers were retained and grouped into six application areas: performance estimation, performance optimization, scheduling, surrogate modeling, fault detection, and language-model-based automation. Scheduling is the most active area, spanning research-oriented reinforcement-learning schedulers to production-friendly hybrids that combine ML with heuristics. Supervised performance estimation is founda- tional for both scheduling and optimization. Graph neural networks and time-series models strengthen anomaly detection by capturing spatio-temporal dependencies in production telemetry. Domain-specialized language models for HPC can outperform general-purpose LLMs on targeted coding and automation tasks. Together, these findings highlight integration opportunities such as LLM-based operating-system concepts and underscore the need for advances in MLOps, standardization of AI components, and benchmarking methodology. 1. JSON: Name: llm_os_orchestrated_hpc_scheduling Title: LLM-OS orchestration of performance estimators, anomaly detectors, and optimizers for scheduling on heterogeneous HPC clusters Short Hypothesis: An LLM-OS that ingests telemetry and supervised performance estimates and issues coordinated scheduling actions will reduce average job completion time by at least 20% relative to SLURM backfill on replayed heterogeneous HPC workloads under identical resource constraints. Related Work: Prior work divides into three families: (1) supervised performance estimation models that predict job runtime, memory, and resource needs to inform placement; (2) reinforcement-learning (RL) and heuristic schedulers that select placements and preemption policies, demonstrating gains in simulation but limited production adoption due to scale, interpretability, and retraining needs; and (3) graph/time-series anomaly detectors and MLOps prototypes that enable proactive maintenance. Separately, proposals for LLM-based system layers describe natural-language orchestration and memory-augmented context handling, but there is no empirical integration of LLM orchestration with production-grade estimators, anomaly detectors, and optimizers in a live scheduling pipeline. Limitations in current approaches include: RL schedulers often require costly simulators and do not generalize across cluster topologies; supervised estimators suffer from dataset and hardware shift; anomaly detectors trade precision for recall without actionable integration; and MLOps/standardization for combining these components is immature. There is no demonstrated end-to-end system that uses an LLM-style orchestrator to coordinate specialized AI agents for scheduling decisions in heterogeneous HPC. Abstract: We propose to evaluate an LLM-OS orchestration layer that integrates specialized AI agents (supervised job performance estimators, GNN/time-series anomaly predictors, and a parameter optimizer) to produce coordinated scheduling actions for heterogeneous HPC clusters. The system converts telemetry and estimator outputs into a compact reasoning context, has the LLM select agent calls and scheduling directives, and issues placements through a scheduler interface. The main contribution is an empirical study that measures whether LLM-driven orchestration improves scheduling outcomes when compared with established baselines. We implement the orchestration layer as a low-latency agent caller, connect it to production-style estimators and detectors, and evaluate via trace replay and controlled cluster experiments. Expected outcomes are quantified reductions in job completion time and energy consumption, characterization of the orchestration overhead, and ablations that reveal the LLM’s role versus rule-based orchestration. The study aims to clarify integration trade-offs and identify failure modes for LLM-enabled HPC control. Experiments: Datasets: (1) Public batch-trace archives: Lublin/SWF subset (HPC2N, SDSC-SP2, BLUE), Microsoft or SenseTime traces where available, and NERSC/ALCF scaled traces; (2) synthetic/AI workloads: ImageNet (ResNet-50), BERT pretraining, GPT-style large-model microbenchmarks; (3) telemetry: simulated or recorded node-level time-series (CPU/GPU util, memory, network, temperature, power) at 1-5 minute granularity. Baselines: (A) SLURM backfill (default heuristics), (B) SLURM backfill augmented with supervised estimator-based requested-time correction, (C) State-of-the-art RL scheduler from literature (trained in simulator), (D) Rule-based orchestrator that routes estimator outputs to scheduler without LLM. Metrics: average job completion time (JCT), median JCT, makespan, average energy consumed (kWh), mean job slowdown, scheduler CPU/RAM overhead, decision latency (ms), fairness (Jain index), anomaly detection AUC, false positive rate, and number of preemptions. Experimental setup: implement LLM-OS as an agent-caller service exposing (i) performance estimator (XGBoost + transformer regressor), (ii) GNN anomaly predictor, (iii) Bayesian optimizer for per-job config; orchestrator receives 5-min aggregated telemetry and estimator outputs and issues placement decisions via a SLURM plugin or CQSim interface. Run two evaluation modes: (1) trace-replay on HPCSim/CQSim with topology variants (homogeneous CPU, mixed CPU+GPU, multi-GPU nodes) and 30 randomized seeds per trace; (2) controlled cluster experiments on a 64-node testbed (mixed GPU types) with injected faults and synthetic DL jobs. Ablations: remove LLM (rule-based), remove anomaly detector, remove estimator, and add noisy/shifted telemetry to measure robustness. Statistical analysis: paired tests (Wilcoxon signed-rank and t-test where applicable) across seeds; report 95% confidence intervals. Success criterion: mean JCT reduction >= 20% versus baseline (A) with p<0.05. Risk Factors and Limitations: LLM hallucination and inconsistency: the LLM may generate inappropriate or invalid scheduler commands, causing suboptimal placements or job failures. Latency and resource overhead: the orchestration layer and LLM inference may introduce decision latency that degrades scheduling responsiveness for short jobs. Data distribution shift: supervised estimators and GNN detectors trained on historical traces may degrade under unseen workloads, hardware, or software stack changes. Security and privacy: telemetry and logs may contain sensitive information; LLM access expands the attack surface and risks data leakage. Compute cost and reproducibility: training and running LLM orchestration and auxiliary models require nontrivial compute, complicating reproducibility and operational deployment. Limited generalization: results on replayed traces and a 64-node testbed may not transfer to larger national-scale centers with different topologies and policies. Evaluation bias: public traces may under-represent modern AI-heavy workloads or specific accelerator heterogeneity, biasing measured gains. Catastrophic scheduling actions: incorrect orchestration could concentrate load or violate constraints, increasing job failure rates or energy spikes.
